How Large Language Models Work
1. What Is a Large Language Model
A Large Language Model (LLM) is a type of neural network trained on massive amounts of text data
to predict the next word, or more precisely the next token, in a sequence. Despite this relatively
simple training objective, LLMs learn to capture grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and even some
limited problem-solving ability purely from statistical patterns in the training data.
Modern LLMs are built on the Transformer architecture, introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All
You Need'. The Transformer replaced earlier recurrent architectures like RNNs and LSTMs with a
mechanism called self-attention, which allows the model to weigh the relevance of every other token
in a sequence when processing a given token, regardless of distance between them.

LLMs are typically trained in multiple stages. The first stage, pretraining, involves training the model
on a very large, diverse corpus of text using the next-token prediction objective. This stage requires
enormous computational resources and is where the model acquires most of its general knowledge
and language ability.
The second stage, often called fine-tuning or instruction tuning, involves further training the model on
smaller, curated datasets of instructions and desired responses, teaching the model to follow user
instructions more reliably.
A third stage, commonly Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), uses human
preference data to further align model outputs with what humans consider helpful, honest, and
harmless, by training a reward model and using it to fine-tune the LLM's behavior.

During inference, the model generates text one token at a time. At each step, it produces a probability

Tokenization and Text Preprocessing
From raw documents to model-ready text
Purpose
This short reference note is written for learning, semantic retrieval, and grounded question-answering experiments.
It uses original explanatory content and is organized into coherent sections rather than unrelated filler.
1. What Tokenization Does
Tokenization converts text into units a model can process. A tokenizer may split a word into one token or several
subword pieces. For example, an uncommon technical term might be represented by multiple fragments rather
than a single token. Token IDs are vocabulary indices, not semantic scores. The embedding layer later maps these
IDs to vectors.
2. Why Subword Tokenization Is Useful
A vocabulary containing every possible word would be huge and would struggle with new names, spelling
variations, and technical terms. Subword methods balance vocabulary size with coverage. Common strings can
remain intact while rare words are decomposed into reusable pieces. This

overage. Common strings can
remain intact while rare words are decomposed into reusable pieces. This is especially useful for scientific writing,
code, product names, and multilingual text. Different model families use different tokenization algorithms and
vocabularies, so token counts can differ for the same passage.
3. Characters, Words, Tokens, and Chunks
Characters, words, model tokens, and retrieval chunks are different units. A 1,000-character passage is not
necessarily a fixed number of tokens. A chunk is a segment selected by an application for storage and retrieval; it
may be defined by characters, tokens, sentences, or document structure. When comparing chunking strategies,
record the actual method and parameters rather than assuming that a character limit corresponds to a universal
token count.
